paragraphs.en: I moved to the little town on the [[seacoast]] in early [[June]], with one heavy suitcase and a thin [[burse]].
The [[vacancy]] at the museum had been advertised for months, and the [[realtor]] who found me a room warned that the town was [[usually]] quiet until July.
[[Already]] the streets were [[rather]] [[empty]], and the only [[shopper]] I passed carried a paper bag and wore a light [[jacket]] against the wind.
My suitcase was over the airline's [[weight]] limit, so I paid a small fine and laughed at my own packing.
As a new [[resident]], I promised myself to walk everywhere and to learn the names of the streets before the [[vacation]] season began.
The [[museum]] was a low stone building at the foot of a [[cliff]], with an old [[telescope]] on the roof pointed at the sea.
Inside, the air smelled of old [[cloth]] and floor polish, and a [[skull]] of some sea creature hung above the stairs.
A [[fossil]] fish lay in a slab of [[stone]] like a shadow frozen in glass.
I had studied [[anatomy]] and [[physiology]] at university, so the bones were not a [[mystery]] to me.
Yet the [[ancient]] handwritten labels made me feel like a beginner again, and I wanted to [[discover]] who had made them.
The director, Mrs. Hale, was [[retiring]] in the autumn after forty years, and she wore a heavy wool [[cloak]] even indoors.
She was [[formidable]] in a quiet way: [[frank]] about money, [[sceptical]] (or [[skeptical]]) of fashionable theories, and full of [[refined]] manners.
She could [[excel]] at almost any practical task, and her [[skill]] with a broken display case was [[undoubted]].
Her [[discipline]] was legendary: she arrived at seven, opened the shutters, and read every label aloud.
She never [[profess]]ed to love the past for its own sake; she simply refused to let it fall apart.
A [[savvy]] old woman, she knew every donor and every grudge in town.
When I asked about the future, she said only, 'Watch, listen, and learn.'
My first task was a [[request]] for a larger [[reserve]] for repairs.
The [[exchequer]] had cut our [[monetary]] support again, and the [[percentage]] was small only on paper.
Every [[fraction]] of a pound mattered, and the [[insurance]] on the collection had risen sharply.
The repair bills were long [[overdue]], and Mrs. Hale talked about [[proportionality]]: a small museum, she said, should not be judged by the size of its grant.
The [[situation]] would [[require]] hard choices, and I spent the evening making lists.
Then a [[benefactor]] appeared, a retired teacher who offered to [[buy]] us a new display case.
The gift did not [[disappoint]] me, but it soon [[became|become]] a small [[scandal]].
A rival paper claimed that our accounts were full of [[corruption]] and that someone had been [[hacking]] our website.
Mrs. Hale refused to [[disclose]] the donor's name, and her calm [[disapproval]] of the rumours only made them louder.
I learned that even a kind act can be twisted into an [[excuse]] for gossip.
The town held a [[forum]] in the church hall, and a [[spokesperson]] for the council agreed to [[show]] up.
The room was full of [[buzz]] and [[wordy]] speeches; people wanted an [[answer]], not a lecture.
I had prepared an [[anecdote]] about our school visits, and I used it to [[respond]] to a rude question.
Later a radio [[anchor]] invited me to [[discourse]] on air for five minutes, and I nearly lost my voice.
That night I wrote down everything I had said and wished I had said half of it.
The new exhibition was to compare a [[tribe]] in [[Asia]] with a [[civilization]] in [[Britain]] and a [[republic]] in old [[France]].
The carved figures and painted bowls told a story about [[procreation]], harvest and [[myth]].
Old labels often [[idealized]] the past and present ancient life as a golden age.
Slavery was a [[by-product]] of that [[civilization]], and the [[slave]] in the corner of the painting had no name.
We decided not to [[foster]] a comfortable [[myth]]; we would show the whole picture, even the shameful parts.
In the back room I began to [[examine]] a box of bones that had never been catalogued.
The [[process]] was slow: [[pick]] up each [[piece]], [[flip]] it over, and [[picture]] where it once belonged.
A [[slice]] of [[stone]] showed a [[fracture]] that had healed long before the animal died.
I tried to [[simulate]] the fall that caused it, using a [[formula]] from my student [[research]].
Seen from another [[angle]], the [[swath]] of [[dirt]] on the surface was the record of a single storm.
A fossil cannot [[reproduce]] anything, but it can [[produce]] a lost climate in your mind.
[[Instead]] of guessing, I wrote a [[direct]] [[example]] beside each item and dated every note.
My days settled into a [[busy]] rhythm: open the doors at nine, [[sit]] at the desk, and watch the [[clock]].
At [[mealtime]] I would [[sip]] weak tea and [[treat]] myself to a bun from the bakery next door.
There was [[ample]] time to read, and for an [[instant]] I would forget the budget.
[[Instead]] of lunch, I sometimes walked along the shore and counted the fishing boats.
It was a small treat, but it kept me calm.
One afternoon a [[troublemaker]] came in with a [[phony]] membership card.
He tried a [[trick]]: he would distract me with a [[trivial]] question and then [[skip]] past the rope.
I felt a [[slight]] [[anger]] rise, but I kept my voice low.
His [[excuse]] was that he was doing research, but his [[slack]] posture and [[whatever]] answers [[disconcert]]ed me.
I did not [[bypass]] the rules; I asked him to leave.
Later I found a [[weakness]] in our own system: the back door was often left open.
[[Mystery]] is good for a museum, but [[trouble]] is not.
On Sunday I [[climb]]ed the path above the [[cliff]] and sat under a wind-bent [[tree]].
The [[cloud]]s moved fast, and the wind seemed to [[excite]] the gulls.
The [[uplifting]] [[music]] on my phone made me [[cling]] to the moment, and I was [[deeply]] grateful for the silence.
[[Since]] I had arrived, I had not once regretted the [[move]].
My [[interest]] in the town was growing, and people had begun to [[interact]] with me as a neighbour rather than a stranger.
The most [[interesting]] thing was that nobody asked why I had come.
[[Whatever]] the winter brought, I wanted to stay.
The town's [[fortune]] had once rested on [[coal]], and the mines had closed before I was born.
Now the shops survived on a thin [[profit]], and the [[trend]] was towards holiday rentals.
A new [[suburb]] of holiday flats was spreading along the coast.
Some families were [[jobless]], and the council's [[climate]] of cuts did not help.
There was an [[excess]] of empty houses and a shortage of affordable ones, while [[obesity]] and cheap food were discussed at every meeting.
[[Exercise]] was free, yet few people had the energy to [[exert]] themselves after a long shift.
The museum could not [[depress]] the town's mood, but it could [[reinforce]] its pride.
A single exhibition would not [[overshadow]] the real problems, but it might help people see them more clearly.
The council had promised to [[liberalize]] the rules for small businesses, a promise repeated so often that it had become a slogan.
The exhibition opened on a wet Friday, and to my surprise the hall was full.
Mrs. Hale cut the ribbon with steady hands and said only, 'It is yours now.'
The local paper called it a small [[triumph]].
In the [[conclusion]] of my report I wrote that [[simplicity]] had saved us: fewer objects, clearer labels, more light.
[[Finally]], the [[undoubted]] success of the school visits gave us confidence to go [[further]].
[[Further]] funding arrived in September, and we began to look [[forward]].
The job had [[reshape]]d me; I no longer wanted to [[disappear]] into a big city archive.
[[Except]] for one broken case, nothing went wrong.
A burst pipe in January would have been a [[disaster]], so we fixed the heating before winter.
The museum would [[close]] for two weeks, but it would reopen.
[[Deprive]]d of money, we had still managed to make something lasting.
In October the trustees agreed to [[decentralise]] (or [[decentralize]]) part of the collection, lending pieces to village halls.
We wrote a simple [[code]] for handling objects, short enough for a volunteer to learn in a morning.
The [[direct]] benefit was obvious: more people saw the collection, and fewer objects sat in the dark.
I learned to [[trim]] a label without losing its meaning.
My last week was spent [[flip]]ping through the visitor book, reading comments in children's handwriting.
Whatever [[resource]]s the next curator had, I hoped she would keep the back door locked.
